title: St George's Day
when_text: 23 April; moved later in the churches' calendars when it falls in Holy Week or Easter week
intro: St George, a soldier-martyr of the eastern Roman empire, has been England's patron saint since the fourteenth century, when Edward III put his Order of the Garter under the saint's protection. His day is kept with flags, church services and, lately, festivals; the dragon story is a medieval legend, and some of the history told about the day turns out to be a later invention.

facts.title: Known in England since Bede
facts.text: George reached England through books long before he became its patron: the earliest English mention is in the writings of Bede, and his feast appears in the ninth-century Durham Collectar.

sources.title: Saint George's Day in England (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The earliest documented mention of St George in England comes from the Venerable Bede (d. 735). His feast day is also mentioned in the Durham Collectar, a 9th-century liturgical work.

facts.title: The first church of St George in England
facts.text: The earliest known dedication to George in England is said to be the church at Fordington, now part of Dorchester in Dorset, which is thought to be named in the will of Alfred the Great.

sources.title: Saint George (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The earliest dedication to the saint in England is a church at Fordington, Dorset, that is mentioned in the will of Alfred the Great.

sources.title: Saint George's Day in England (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The will of Alfred the Great is said to refer to the saint, in a reference to the church of Fordington, Dorset.

facts.title: George riding to the rescue at Fordington
facts.text: Over Fordington's south door is a carved Norman tympanum of George on horseback, with soldiers praying on one side and the fallen on the other; it is thought to show the story that he appeared to help the crusaders at Antioch, not the dragon.

sources.title: Church of St George, Dorchester (Historic England list entry 1292171, via British Listed Buildings)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: representing St George, mounted, with praying soldiers on the left and dead or dying soldiers on the right. It allegedly represents St George's miraculous intervention in the Battle of Antioch

facts.title: The synod that did not make his day
facts.text: For centuries the Synod of Oxford, held at Osney Abbey in 1222, was said to have made St George's Day a holy day in England. Historians showed in the 1960s that the earliest manuscripts of its decrees do not mention George at all.

sources.title: Synod of Oxford (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: However, since the 1960s, this has been regarded by historians as an invention.

sources.title: Saint George's Day in England (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In the past, historians mistakenly pointed to the Synod of Oxford in 1222 as elevating the feast to special prominence, but the earliest manuscripts of the synod's declaration do not mention the feast of St George.

facts.title: Patron of the Garter
facts.text: Edward III made George the patron of his new Order of the Garter, reputedly in thanks for help at the battle of Crécy; from then on the saint's red cross banner flew more and more beside the royal arms. Until then Edward the Confessor and Edmund the Martyr had been England's leading saints.

sources.title: Saint George's Day in England (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1348, Edward III gave St George a special position as a patron saint of the Order of the Garter in thanks for his supposed intervention at the Battle of Crécy.

facts.title: New Garter knights on his day
facts.text: The monarch's choice of new Knights and Ladies of the Garter is usually announced on St George's Day; they are installed later, at the Garter Day service in St George's Chapel each June.

sources.title: Order of the Garter (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Appointments are typically announced on Saint George's Day (23 April).

sources.title: Order of the Garter (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Each June, on Garter Day, the members of the Order, wearing their habits and garter insignia, meet at Windsor Castle.

facts.title: A great feast from 1415
facts.text: The church province of Canterbury raised St George's Day to a 'double major feast' in 1415, the year of Agincourt, and York followed in 1421.

sources.title: Saint George's Day in England (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: St George's Day was elevated to a "double major feast" in the declarations of the Province of Canterbury in 1415 and the Province of York in 1421

facts.title: The one saint's banner the Reformation spared
facts.text: When the English Reformation did away with religious banners, George's was the only saint's flag allowed to stay. His cross is first recorded as an English flag at sea in 1545.

sources.title: Saint George's Day in England (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The position of St George as patron saint of England was respected during the English Reformation, when all other religious flags were abolished, including all saints' banners, except for his.

sources.title: Saint George's Day in England (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The first recorded use of St. George's Cross as an English maritime flag, in conjunction with royal banners, dates to 1545.

facts.title: Where the dragon died
facts.text: Local legend puts George's fight with the dragon on Dragon Hill, the flat-topped knoll below the Uffington White Horse, and says the bare patch of chalk on top, where no grass grows, is where the dragon's blood was spilt.

sources.title: Dragon Hill, Uffington (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: According to legend, Saint George slew the dragon here. A bare patch of chalk upon which no grass will grow is purported to be where the dragon's blood spilled.

facts.title: Shakespeare's day too
facts.text: Shakespeare died on 23 April 1616, and his unknown birthday is traditionally kept on the same date, St George's Day; all that is recorded is his baptism on 26 April 1564 at Holy Trinity, Stratford, where he is also buried.

sources.title: William Shakespeare (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: His date of birth is unknown but is traditionally observed on 23 April, Saint George's Day.

sources.title: Church of the Holy Trinity, Stratford-upon-Avon (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: William Shakespeare, poet and playwright, was baptised in Holy Trinity on 26 April 1564 and was buried there on 25 April 1616.

facts.title: George in the mummers' play
facts.text: In most folk plays of the mummers the hero is Saint George (or King or Prince George), who fights an opponent and is set right by a quack doctor. Oddly, the dragon hardly ever comes on stage; the earliest hint of such a play is a scrap of a George speech from Exeter that may date from 1737.

sources.title: Mummers' play (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Despite the frequent presence of Saint George, the Dragon rarely appears although it is often mentioned.

sources.title: Mummers' play (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: a fragmentary speech by St George from Exeter, Devon, which may date from 1737

facts.title: St George in Shetland
facts.text: The sword dance of Papa Stour in Shetland was introduced by a rhyme spoken by St George as master of the Seven Champions of Christendom; Walter Scott printed it in 1831, from a performance of about 1788.

sources.title: Mummers' play (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1831, Sir Walter Scott published a rhyme which had been used as a prelude to the Papa Stour Sword Dance, Shetland in around 1788.

sources.title: Mummers' play (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: All the characters are introduced in turn by the Master, St. George.

facts.title: A pageant back after 425 years
facts.text: London held what was billed as the first Pageant of St George in 425 years in 2010; it has grown into a festival in Trafalgar Square run by the Mayor of London. Modern efforts to celebrate the day go back to the Royal Society of St George, founded in 1894.

sources.title: Saint George's Day in England (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: announced as "the first Pageant of St George in 425 years"

sources.title: Saint George's Day in England (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: date from the foundation of Royal Society of St. George in 1894

places.name: Dragon Hill, Uffington
places.why: A natural chalk knoll with a levelled top below the White Horse, where legend says George killed the dragon.

sources.title: Dragon Hill, Uffington (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Dragon Hill is a natural chalk hill with an artificially flattened top (on the scarp slope of White Horse Hill).

places.name: Uffington White Horse
places.why: The prehistoric chalk figure above Dragon Hill, on the same hillside; the knoll below it is tied by legend to George.

sources.title: Uffington White Horse (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Dragon Hill is a natural chalk hill with an artificial flat top, associated in legend with St George.

places.name: St George's Chapel, Windsor Castle
places.why: The chapel of the Order of the Garter, whose patron is George; founded by Edward III and rebuilt in the late fifteenth century.

sources.title: St George's Chapel, Windsor Castle (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: St George's Chapel was founded in the 14th century by King Edward III and extensively enlarged in the late 15th century.

places.name: St George's Church, Fordington
places.why: Thought to be the earliest church in England dedicated to George, with a Norman carving of the saint over its south door.

sources.title: Saint George (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The earliest dedication to the saint in England is a church at Fordington, Dorset

sources.title: Church of St George, Dorchester (Historic England list entry 1292171, via British Listed Buildings)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: South doorway has a carved tympanum of Caen stone

places.name: St George's Church, Brinsop
places.why: A Herefordshire church with a carved twelfth-century tympanum of George on horseback killing the dragon, in the style of the Herefordshire school of carvers.

sources.title: Church of St George, Brinsop and Wormsley (Historic England list entry 1081971, via British Listed Buildings)
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: North aisle has excellent mid-C12 sculpture. Tympanum of St George and the Dragon

sources.title: Brinsop (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: depicts St George on horseback, a knight crusader slaying a serpent-dragon

places.name: Osney Abbey
places.why: Site of the Synod of Oxford of 1222, long but wrongly credited with making St George's Day a holy day.

sources.title: Synod of Oxford (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Synod of Oxford was held on 9 May 1222, at Osney Abbey, in Oxford, England.

places.name: Holy Trinity Church, Stratford-upon-Avon
places.why: Where Shakespeare, whose birthday is kept on St George's Day and who died on it, was baptised and buried.

sources.title: Church of the Holy Trinity, Stratford-upon-Avon (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: He is buried in the 15th-century chancel built by Thomas Balsall

places.name: Shakespeare's Birthplace
places.why: The house in Henley Street, Stratford, where Shakespeare is believed to have been born; his birthday is celebrated in the town on 23 April.

sources.title: Shakespeare's Birthplace (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: where it is believed that William Shakespeare was born in 1564 and spent his childhood years

sources.title: Saint George's Day in England (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: 23 April is widely recognised as his traditional date of birth and commemorated on this day every year in his home Stratford upon Avon and throughout the world.

places.name: Papa Stour
places.why: Shetland island whose sword dance, led by St George as master of the Seven Champions, was written down by Walter Scott.

sources.title: Papa Stour (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Papa Stour sword dance may be of Norse origin and bears similarities to the long sword dance of the north east of England.
